planting.note: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; nutmeg is a true tropical rainforest tree that needs consistent warmth, humidity, and shelter from wind and is only realistic outdoors in frost-free zone 11 or as a large container specimen kept above 60°F year-round elsewhere.

directions: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; nutmeg is a true tropical rainforest tree that needs consistent warmth, humidity, and shelter from wind and is only realistic outdoors in frost-free zone 11 or as a large container specimen kept above 60°F year-round elsewhere. Native to the Banda Islands of Indonesia, this evergreen tree bears apricot-like fruit that splits open to reveal a hard seed wrapped in a bright red, lacy covering; the seed itself is dried and ground into nutmeg, while the red aril is separately dried and ground into mace, making a single fruit the source of two distinct spices. Trees are dioecious, so both a male pollinator and a female fruiting tree (or a grafted tree combining both) are needed for fruit production, and trees typically take seven to nine years to begin bearing and up to twenty years to reach full production. Grow in the dappled shade of taller trees as it would experience in its native rainforest understory, keep humidity high, and protect from any cold below the mid-50s Fahrenheit.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky to sandy, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; caper bush is a Mediterranean cliff-dwelling plant that rots in rich, moist, or poorly drained soil and thrives on neglect once established.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky to sandy, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; caper bush is a Mediterranean cliff-dwelling plant that rots in rich, moist, or poorly drained soil and thrives on neglect once established. Sprawling, spiny stems carry rounded, fleshy, blue-green leaves and large, showy, white-to-pink flowers with a prominent burst of long purple stamens, opening for just a single day each but produced continuously through the hot summer months. The edible product is the unopened flower bud, hand-picked daily at pea size and brine- or salt-cured into the tangy, briny capers used in Mediterranean cooking; unpicked buds open into flowers and later develop into a caper-berry fruit that can also be pickled. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once its deep taproot is established, it is well suited to a rock wall, dry slope, or container where poor soil and reflected heat are assets rather than liabilities, and it dies back to the root in hard freezes, resprouting the following spring in marginal zones.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; kava is a Pacific Island understory plant that is sterile and propagated only from cuttings, and it needs warmth, humidity, and shelter from direct sun and wind.

directions: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; kava is a Pacific Island understory plant that is sterile and propagated only from cuttings, and it needs warmth, humidity, and shelter from direct sun and wind. This large, heart-leaved shrub has been cultivated for centuries across Polynesia, Melanesia, and Micronesia, where its thick roots are pounded and mixed with water to produce a traditional ceremonial and social beverage valued for its mild relaxant effect. It requires consistently warm, humid, frost-free conditions and rich, well-drained soil in filtered light, essentially replicating the sheltered forest-garden conditions of its native Pacific islands, and struggles badly with cold, dry air or direct hot sun. Roots are typically harvested for use after three to five years of growth; further north than zone 10, it must be grown as a protected container plant moved indoors well before any cold weather.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this understory ginger relative needs the warm, humid, sheltered conditions of a tropical forest floor and is not frost-tolerant.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this understory ginger relative needs the warm, humid, sheltered conditions of a tropical forest floor and is not frost-tolerant. A clumping, cane-forming member of the ginger family native to the forest understories of southern China and Southeast Asia, it produces small flowers low on the rhizomes near the soil surface, followed by reddish-brown, spiny-husked seed capsules that are dried and used as a substitute for true cardamom in traditional Chinese medicine and cooking, with a similar but more camphorous, less refined aroma. Its broad, glossy, tropical foliage and shade tolerance make it a useful textural understory plant in a warm, humid shade garden even where the spice itself is not harvested. Divide congested clumps in spring to propagate and maintain vigor, and protect from any temperature below the mid-40s Fahrenheit.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; beach wormwood is adapted to coastal dunes and tolerates salt spray and wind but rots quickly in heavy, wet, or richly amended soil.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; beach wormwood is adapted to coastal dunes and tolerates salt spray and wind but rots quickly in heavy, wet, or richly amended soil. Deeply lobed, densely white-woolly leaves form a low, spreading mat that brightens a border with silvery foliage color all season, topped in summer by small, inconspicuous yellow flower clusters that many gardeners simply shear off to keep the foliage display tidy. Native to sand dunes and gravelly beaches of the northeastern coasts of North America and northeastern Asia, it spreads by rhizome to stabilize loose, sandy soil and is outstanding for seaside gardens, dune plantings, and hot, dry, sandy sites where richer plants fail. It tolerates salt spray, wind, and drought better than the related, more commonly grown dusty miller (Jacobaea maritima) and is fully winter hardy in cold coastal climates.
